title: The Ten Thousand Offices of Heaven
subtitle: Heaven, ancestors, spirits and the dead in Tianzhao
summary: Heaven as order, a celestial bureaucracy, the ancestors at breakfast, Collectors who sometimes get the name wrong, gods who can be reviewed, and whether Heaven reaches beyond the Gates.
content:
> *"You do not have permission to enter."*
> — the sense of a common talisman

Tianzhao has no single church that corresponds neatly to the Aurelian Crowned Sun or the Kharadi Covenant. Its religious life is an overlapping ecosystem: Heaven, the ancestors, local gods, divine officials, spirits, philosophical schools, household rites, the courts of the dead and traditions of reincarnation, all existing side by side.

A person in Tianzhao may honour their ancestors in the morning, petition the city god at noon, consult a physician in the afternoon, study philosophy in the evening and call in a spirit specialist when the house starts making noises at night, and see no contradiction in any of it. Asked *"Which of these is your true religion?"*, many Tianzhao people would find the question strange, or simply too narrow.

This entry describes that world of belief. It is belief: nothing in Tianzhao's rites has ever been shown to work as magic, and the Gates remain the only source of magic anyone has found. For the state that administers part of it, see [[the-tianzhao-mandate|The Tianzhao Mandate]].

## Heaven and the Three Realms

**Heaven** is Tianzhao's highest idea of cosmic order. It is not necessarily a personal god with a face and a will. Heaven is order itself: legitimacy, right relationship, the greater structure of things. Even the most powerful celestial beings are not automatically the same thing as Heaven.

A widespread popular cosmology describes **Three Realms**: the **Mortal Realm**, the **Spirit Realm** and the **Celestial Realm**. Their boundaries are permeable. Contact or movement between them can happen through dreams, death, ritual, sacred places and supernatural manifestations. The Three Realms are influential, but they are not a single agreed system, and different schools describe them differently.

## The Celestial Bureaucracy

Tianzhao imagines the supernatural order in bureaucratic terms. There may be powers responsible for rivers, cities, mountains, roads, households, storms, harvests, scholarship, war, medicine, dreams, childbirth, craft, justice and death. They may be ancient spirits, elevated mortals, divine officials, local gods or old powers who have been granted rank.

Different traditions classify the same being in different ways, and Tianzhao is comfortable with that. A river spirit may be an official to one school and an ancient power to another, and still be owed the same courtesy by the people who live on its banks.

### Five well-loved figures

- **The Jade Chancellor** presides over divine law, cosmic administration, records, appointments and legitimacy. The Jade Chancellor is immensely powerful, but is **not** Heaven, and is not the creator of the world. Even the highest office is an office.
- **Lady Shun, Keeper of Names**, watches over ancestry, memory, genealogy, burial records and the identities of the dead. In Tianzhao a forgotten or wrongly recorded dead person can become a serious spiritual problem, and Lady Shun is invoked wherever records of the dead are kept.
- **General Bao, Lord of the Red Gate**, is the guardian of thresholds, gates, walls and fortifications, and the patron of soldiers, guards and courage against hostile spirits. Since the Gates appeared, his image has become hugely popular among soldiers, guards and Expeditioners. The connection is cultural: nothing suggests he has anything to do with the Valeoran Gates themselves.
- **Mistress Lin of Ten Thousand Remedies** is the patron of medicine, herbs, physicians, poisons, healing and difficult diagnosis. Legend says she tasted every medicinal plant in the world, and some stories say she died, returned and carried on working. Physicians tell those stories with affection and do not insist on them.
- **The Laughing Magistrate** stands for mediation, common sense, local justice, the exposure of hypocrisy and satire. The Magistrate's stories are about rigid procedure being defeated by practical wisdom and clever reading. The Magistrate is not against the law, but stands for the law working as it was meant to, rather than becoming ridiculous.

## The Ancestors

Ancestor practice is the heart of everyday religion in Tianzhao. Families keep shrines, records, offerings, incense and memorial tablets. The ancestors remain connected to their family, household and descendants. They may protect and advise. They may also become lonely or troubled, and need attention. Exactly what the ancestors are, and where, differs between families and schools.

> **An ordinary morning in a Tianzhao household**
>
> Before breakfast, the grandmother lit three sticks of incense at the family shrine and set down a small dish of rice and a cup of tea.
>
> "Your great-grandfather's boat is being repaired today," she told the tablets, in the same voice she used for the neighbours. "The boy says it will cost too much. I said it will cost less than a new one." She straightened the cup. "And the cat has been sick on the stairs again. I mention it in case anyone knows why."
>
> Then she went to make breakfast. Nobody in the house thought any of it was unusual.

## Ghosts, Collectors and the Courts of the Dead

Not every dead person becomes a **ghost**. Ghosts are a failure or interruption in the proper passage of the dead, and they may result from violent death, improper burial, unresolved obligations, a forgotten identity, strong attachment or interference with ritual.

The dead are guided by the **Collectors**, also called the **Officers of Passage**. Collectors do not normally cause death. They arrive after it, identify the deceased, and guide them toward the appropriate court. They are pictured in robes and official hats, sometimes masked, carrying chains, tablets, registers and lanterns. Stories show them as terrifying, solemn, exhausted or simply irritated by paperwork, and sometimes all four.

The dead may pass through **courts** that examine their actions, relationships, obligations, the harms they did and the attachments they kept. These courts are not only places of punishment. Depending on the school, they judge, purify, place, prepare for reincarnation, return the dead to their ancestry, or assign them service in the spirit world. **Reincarnation** is widely believed in, though not in one agreed form, and folk stories tell of children who remember earlier lives, unusual birthmarks, forgotten names and inherited habits.

> **The Wrong Name, a story told in many villages (one common version)**
>
> The Collector arrived at the farmhouse at dusk, unrolled the register and read out the farmer's name.
>
> "There must be a mistake," said the farmer.
>
> "There is no mistake. It is in the register." The Collector ran a long finger down the column. "Farmer, of this village, with two oxen, a wife, three children and..." He frowned. "Four goats."
>
> "I have three goats."
>
> The Collector looked at the register. He looked at the goat pen. He counted. He counted again.
>
> "This is most irregular," he said, and rolled up the register, and went away to have it corrected.
>
> The next morning the farmer walked to market and bought a fourth goat. Then a fifth, to be safe. The story says he lived another thirty years, and the Collector, when he finally came back, was in a very bad mood.

The Wrong Name is folklore, not theology, and nobody in Tianzhao treats it as doctrine. Its point is the joke: bureaucracy reaches even into the afterlife, and bureaucracy makes mistakes.

## Spirits of Places and Things

Spirits may emerge from, or attach themselves to, natural places, objects, things used again and again, strong emotion, and things that matter to a community. Swords, trees and houses have their spirits in the old stories.

Tianzhao folklore does not stand still. Newer stories speak of spirits of **railways**, **factories**, **telegraph lines** and even **elevators**. Whether such spirits truly arise from machines, or whether the stories are simply how a very old culture makes room for very new things, is argued over. Either way, Tianzhao folklore grows alongside its technology.

## Recognition, Review and Demotion

The state's **Registry of Recognized Powers** may recognise, register and title local supernatural powers, and in principle demote them. A god who consistently fails in their recognised duties can become the subject of petitions, ritual complaints and administrative review. It sounds like a joke to foreigners. In Tianzhao it is meant quite seriously, though nobody pretends it is never funny. How such reviews proceed is not set down here.

> **A petition to the prefectural office of Ritual & Anomalous Affairs (as filed)**
>
> *From the elders of the village at the lower ford.*
>
> *We respectfully submit that the Lord of the Little River, recognised by this office with title and temple, has for three successive years permitted the river to flood the bridge, the mill and the lower fields, despite proper offerings on every occasion required.*
>
> *We do not accuse the Lord of malice. We note only that the duties of the title have not been performed.*
>
> *We therefore request a review of the title, or, failing that, assistance with the bridge.*
>
> *Either would be acceptable.*

## Talismans and True Names

Written words carry great weight in Tianzhao: names, seals, talismans and official inscriptions. A talisman is often understood less as a raw spell than as **an assertion of recognised authority**, a notice that something has no right to be where it is. The sense of many of them is simply: *you do not have permission to enter.* Foreigners frequently cannot tell a religious inscription from a bureaucratic notice or a containment warning, and the overlap is not an accident.

**Names** can establish identity, relationship and authority, so Tianzhao people are cautious about giving their full formal name to an unknown supernatural being. Since the Gates opened, Tianzhao researchers have started applying the same caution to beings encountered beyond them. Whether a name truly gives power over its owner is a matter of ritual belief and debate, not established fact.

## Dragons, Foxes and the Painted Door

Tianzhao **dragons** are associated with water, rivers, storms, rainfall and the sea, and with authority and wisdom. They are not monsters to be slain. Angering a dragon is as much an administrative, ritual and diplomatic problem as a military one.

**Fox spirits** may be shapeshifters, tricksters, lovers, manipulators, sources of knowledge or protectors. Their stories teach one lesson above all: *something that looks human may not think like a human.* They are neither good nor evil as a rule.

One old tale has become newly interesting. In the story of **the Painted Door**, a scholar steps into a palace painted on a door or screen, attends a feast at a strange court, makes an impossible journey, and returns to find that decades have passed. Since the Gates opened, some researchers have begun to wonder whether stories like this preserve distorted memories of something Gate-like. Others say a story is a story. Nothing has been confirmed.

## Festivals of the Dead

During the **Hungry Ghost Festival**, the boundary between the living and the dead is believed to grow thin. Families make offerings, hang lanterns, hold performances and leave empty seats for unseen guests. The details vary from region to region.

The **Festival of Returning Names** is for those who died with no descendants or surviving family. Their names are recited aloud, so that they do not disappear entirely. The archives kept for it are extraordinarily valuable, and the University of Verna would very much like broader scholarly access to them. Tianzhao has not been in a hurry to grant it.

## Foreign Gods

Tianzhao is relatively relaxed about meeting foreign religions, and its scholars tend to try to fit foreign powers into existing categories. This can irritate the foreigners. A First Light priest does not always enjoy learning that a Lantern-Bearer has been assigned a provisional administrative rank. When they object, the Tianzhao answer is usually some version of: *the appropriate classification has not yet been determined.*

## Heaven and the Gates

The Gates have raised what may be the most serious metaphysical question in Tianzhao's long history: **does Heaven govern beyond the Gates?**

If it does, then Tianzhao's understanding of Heaven was too small. If it does not, Heaven may not be universal at all. A third position holds that Heaven was never a single territorial celestial government in the first place, but the principle of ordered relationship itself, which different worlds might express in different ways. The question is open.

Four broad theories about the Gate worlds are argued over:

- **Distant Provinces.** Gate worlds are far-off regions of the same greater cosmic order. Humanity simply understood the universe too narrowly.
- **Outer Spirit Realms.** Gate worlds belong somewhere within or beside the known spiritual reality, unusual extensions of the Spirit Realm rather than separate creations.
- **Foreign Heavens.** Gate worlds have their own ordered supernatural structures: different spirit hierarchies, different divine administrations, different metaphysical relationships.
- **Heavenless Places.** The most controversial idea: that some Gate worlds may lie outside the order Tianzhao calls Heaven altogether. The phrase is unofficial, uncomfortable and not doctrine.

### The Collector at the Gate

One of the most repeated and most disturbing stories of the Gate era claims that a Collector came to a Gate threshold and refused to cross, saying:

> *"Beyond this door, your name is not in my register."*

The account is unauthenticated and disputed. It is also everywhere. Its power lies in the fear it expresses: that Tianzhao's spiritual order, the order that guides its dead and keeps its names, might have limits to its jurisdiction.

> **In a tea house near the Pavilion of Celestial Affairs**
>
> The Expeditioner had told the story three times that evening, and it got better each time. "...and it stood at the threshold, with its lantern, and it said: *beyond this door, your name is not in my register.*"
>
> The table was silent.
>
> Then the young scholar from the Pavilion put down her cup.
>
> "Who witnessed it?"
>
> "Well, a friend of a crewman who..."
>
> "Who, specifically? Name, date, which Gate, which crew. Was the Collector seen, or heard, or inferred? By whom?" She took out a notebook. "If it is true, it is the most important thing anyone has said in this city. So I would like to know who said it."
>
> The Expeditioner found he had somewhere else to be.
